: **Residual-claims register for the aisle and the pick station**: Proposed responses to three open premises behind the mobile manipulator's aisle speed and its pick; operating credit requires the supporting evidence stipulated in the restricted-service branch. For each, the register names the missing physical observable, the hazard it permits, the operating restriction and its accountable owner, and the predeclared closure test that would retire the restriction. {#tbl-17-claims-register tbl-colwidths="[22,24,26,28]"}

The register also retains the unresolved timing premise from @sec-placement. Capture-to-dispatch age does not include dispatch-to-admission work, and nominal inference cadence does not bound the interval between successful admissions. The runtime team owns a loaded qualification of both intervals against the handoff record's lease and renewal requirements. Until that evidence and a positive required reserve support the complete stop, the normal aisle speed remains a candidate. The stipulated service branch assumes supporting timing evidence for its restricted mode; it does not close this item in the actual records.

A release pipeline records each entry in a fixed schema, and its fields, units, and invariants appear with the other record layouts in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-residual-claims.

#### Maintaining the restrictions {#sec-frontier-operationalizing-claims}

The restrictions in the register must reach the mechanisms that govern deployment and execution. A signed speed ceiling constrains the permission path; an inspection requirement constrains site operations. The release pipeline checks that both belong to the authorized configuration, while runtime monitors check only those conditions their sensors can establish. An unobserved premise cannot become a measured condition merely because it appears in a machine-readable record.

An updated model or configuration must retain every standing restriction whose supporting claim remains unchanged. The deployment gate validates the signed limits and the evidence status before authorizing a mode. A restricted mode needs its own supported release; an open entry does not automatically authorize a downgrade. Runtime checks can enforce the speed ceiling and current authority, while site operations maintains the floor and feed procedures at their specified cadences.

The selected fallback remains the state-dependent response qualified in @sec-enforcement. A rejected replacement proposal need not revoke an active command whose own evidence, lease, and state remain valid. Loss of active permission does require a feasible response within the remaining budget. Powered deceleration, brake application at standstill, torque inhibit, and supply isolation have different physical effects; the register cannot replace those distinctions with a universal cutoff recipe.

The proposed detectors would support broader online claims only after qualification. Conservative actions, passive limits, proof tests, or a narrower task may support different claims without resolving every hidden state. Choosing among these responses requires checking what can still happen before the physical deadline.

### Failures without detectors {#sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors}

A floor-film detector can change the friction claim only if its coverage, false alarms, and response timing support the intended route. These are task-specific acceptance criteria, not universal detector thresholds. The known-component stopping calculation leaves `{python} OilFilm.spare_aisle_str` at the candidate normal aisle speed, equivalent to `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str` of travel before charging dispatch-to-admission work and preserving the required reserve. This is an upper limit on unallocated time, not a qualified detector budget. It also cannot establish protection against a person who continues approaching throughout the stop.

The floor-film detector faces an even stricter form of the same test. Its forward detection distance, less the travel incurred during its own sensing and inference latency, must cover the dry-floor stop to the film's leading edge. A classification report that arrives once the drive wheels have already crossed onto the film leaves an incomplete stopping budget already at `{python} OilFilm.stop_oil_str` against the `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance. A classification received after that point supports incident diagnosis, but it cannot safeguard the action already taken.

#### Observational indistinguishability and the action deadline {#sec-frontier-observational-indistinguishability-sub}

The fundamental physical limit of runtime detection arises from observational indistinguishability. Consider two physical states of the world, $S_A$ and $S_B$. In state $S_A$, a commanded actuator trajectory $u(t)$ is completely safe. In state $S_B$, the identical trajectory $u(t)$ causes catastrophic structural fracture or human injury, requiring the permission path to intervene and command an immediate stop. Let $t_{\text{harm}}$ denote the harm time under the unchanged trajectory. A conservative latest start time for completing the selected stop before that time subtracts the bounded enforcement, actuation, and braking intervals:
$$t_{\text{deadline}} = t_{\text{harm}} - (t_{\text{enforce}} + t_{\text{actuation}} + t_{\text{brake}}).$$
This planning deadline concerns completion of that response before nominal harm. It is not a universal last opportunity to prevent harm: braking changes the trajectory and therefore can change the harm time itself. Establishing the latest effective intervention requires the coupled motion or contact model. If the telemetry history $y(t)$ provided by onboard instrumentation is identical for $S_A$ and $S_B$ across the entire interval $t \le t_{\text{deadline}}$, no algorithm operating on those observations can reliably distinguish the benign state from the hazardous one. Identical telemetry traces rule out a state-specific response before that deadline. A conservative action chosen for both states or a passive mechanical limit may still protect them, if its own clearance and force assumptions are valid.

#### Responses when the state remains hidden {#sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment}

When physical states are observationally indistinguishable before the deadline, software cannot choose a different response for each state. A conservative action valid in both states can still be admitted. Where no such action exists, mechanical compliance, physical proof-testing, or structural isolation must establish a supported operating envelope, or operation must be withheld.

Sensing hardware shows the same limit over longer durations. A robot's strain-gauge wrist force-torque transducer can drift as mechanical stress relaxation and temperature cycles affect its bridge output, and a transducer whose zero has drifted low reports the same trend as an interaction that genuinely exerts lower contact force. A single channel reports one scalar wrench component, and no algorithm on that signal can tell a changed physical interaction from a degraded calibration baseline. Without an independent reference, such as an unloaded tare or zero-point proof test, that signal alone cannot establish the drift at runtime.[^fn-hw-piezoresistive-drift]

[^fn-hw-piezoresistive-drift]: **Strain-Gauge Transducer Drift**\index{Strain-gauge transducer!drift}: Mechanical stress relaxation, adhesive creep, and temperature cycles can alter a strain-gauge bridge baseline over extended campaigns. Filtering that signal alone cannot distinguish baseline drift from a true change in force. An unloaded tare, a zero-point proof test, or independently calibrated sensing can supply the reference needed to check the force estimate.

The weakened latch at the door is the arm's case of the same limit, and a faster one. Until the latch yields, the joint torque sensors read the same torques against a weakened latch as against a sound one, because both carry the same contact force, and the channel holds no trace of the strength that remains. The yield is irreversible, and no command issued after it restores the latch, so a faster classifier on the joint torque channel protects nothing. The defensible responses supply what that channel lacks. A proof test establishes the latch's strength at a declared interval, and it covers the interval only if corrosion and wear cannot carry the yield force below the contact ceiling between two tests, a rate that the maintenance record, not the torque channel, must support.

A passive compliant element can limit transmitted force over a qualified stroke, but its stiffness, preload, energy capacity, and bottoming behavior must fit the admitted contact. The stiffness condition in @eq-frontier-passive-compliance is one component of that argument:
$$k_{\text{spring}} \le \frac{F_{\text{allow}}-F_{\text{preload}}}{\Delta x_{\text{stall}}}$$ {#eq-frontier-passive-compliance}
where $F_{\text{allow}}$ is the structural yield threshold of the workpiece, $F_{\text{preload}}$ is the preload resisting nominal manipulation forces, and $\Delta x_{\text{stall}}$ is the compliance stroke available before cutting drive power. A buffer that is too stiff or bottoms out can exceed the admitted contact limit before the selected response takes effect. Qualification must test the complete load path and response, not stiffness alone.[^fn-math-contact-lipschitz]

The same choice applies to the packaging cell. A qualified engagement measurement can support automated sign-off; downstream inspection can support a service that makes no autonomous sign-off claim. Either can be useful if the complete workflow meets its declared task criteria. The engineer chooses a response by the claim it supports and the evidence needed to maintain it.

[^fn-math-contact-lipschitz]: **Contact Boundary**\index{Contact mechanics!non-smooth impact}: Rigid impact and friction transitions can invalidate a smooth free-motion model. Peak contact force and component damage require measured stiffness, damping, geometry, and actuator response; neither a controller nor a passive part alone supplies a universal bound.

## Choosing the Next Capability {#sec-frontier-assumptions-change}

The packaging cell's restricted transport and refused sign-off lead to different research investments. Faster proposal serving may improve throughput; a qualified engagement measurement may support autonomous sign-off. Each advance needs a predeclared task result and a test of the premise it changes. Improvement within an existing envelope and evidence for expanding that envelope are related but distinct outcomes.

### Match the experiment to the missing evidence {#sec-frontier-four-gap-classes}

An unmeasured observable calls for a measurement that distinguishes the relevant states before action becomes ineffective. An evaluation deficit calls for trials or estimators that represent the claimed population, with uncertainty and dependence accounted for. A theoretical deficit calls for a bounded argument whose assumptions can be established for the machine. A scope mismatch calls for a changed architecture or a narrower task. These diagnoses choose the next experiment; they do not force every residual claim to have a detector-based solution.

The tail methods collected in @sec-appendix-ml-evt can help evaluate rare exceedances when their distributional assumptions hold. A fitted tail does not establish those assumptions or validate unobserved contact dynamics. Likewise, the reachability methods in @sec-appendix-control-hj-reachability concern a specified plant and disturbance model. Moving an unsupported friction premise into a simulator or certificate does not discharge it.

### Research that changes an engineering result {#sec-frontier-four-open-challenges}

Low-latency proposal serving can improve work completed before goals and observations become stale. Compression, local memory, and separation of slower intent from faster action generation must be assessed through closed-loop task performance under the sustained workload of @sec-placement. With a valid independent fallback, proposer delay can reduce availability without extending the protective response deadline. Shared-resource interference must be tested separately because it can defeat that independence.

More tractable verification can enlarge the set of candidate operating envelopes the engineer can examine. The useful result is a declared property, model, uncertainty range, and measured verification cost, together with evidence that the physical system meets the premises. State dimension alone does not determine verification time, and a network certificate alone does not qualify an assembled machine.

Continual adaptation can recover useful behavior as tires wear, contact conditions change, or tasks expand. New experience must retain provenance, and the changed candidate must pass closed-loop and regression evaluation. Any earlier evidence retained across an update needs a justified dependency and equivalence argument, as in @sec-release. The independent permission path does not lose its justification merely because proposer weights change, but adaptation must not consume resources that path needs.

Multi-robot coordination adds a joint task to these obligations. Delayed shared intent cannot replace the local observations needed for admission. Conservative yielding may avoid an immediate conflict while preventing every robot from making progress, and a shared payload couples their forces. A useful protocol must establish task completion and physical bounds under its declared communication and failure conditions.

Each direction extends the same engineering discipline rather than suspending it. The next capability begins with a concrete task the current machine cannot yet perform, an identified constraint or missing premise, and evidence that would justify the changed design.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-frontier-fallacies-pitfalls}

The warehouse and packaging examples can fail as engineering arguments even when their individual calculations are correct. Three mistakes sever the connection between useful work, physical limits, and evidence.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A protective intervention means the whole machine failed its task.*

A least-change speed correction may let the robot complete its delivery within the permitted envelope. Report raw proposer autonomy separately from whole-machine task success and protective outcomes. Combining them into one failure count obscures whether the next improvement belongs in learning, integration, or the protective response.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating a restriction as evidence that its physical premise holds.*

The oil-film calculation still needs traction after the speed ceiling is reduced. Inspection must have a qualified means of establishing the restricted friction floor and a regime that preserves it; a visually clear route or a signed speed value supplies neither by itself. The actual illustrative release remains refused, while the stipulated service branch demonstrates the consequence of supporting those premises.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *More model capacity or simulated exposure settles every residual claim.*

A better proposer can improve useful behavior, and simulation can expose failures in modeled conditions. Neither supplies a physical observable absent from its inputs or validates a contact property omitted by its model. Select new experience, measurement, a passive limit, or a narrower task according to the missing claim, then evaluate the changed machine.
:::

## Summary {#sec-frontier-summary}

The warehouse mission now has a connected design argument, and the packaging cell shows how to transfer it. Physical budgets define feasible action; traceable experience and closed-loop evaluation establish useful behavior; timely integration preserves that behavior within current limits; release and maintenance keep the service tied to its evidence. The residual-claims register preserves what remains open and directs the next improvement.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Engineering a machine that senses and acts"}

* **Useful service joins the four parts:** Body limits, learned competence, runtime integration, and maintained evidence must support the same task.
* **Competence can grow:** New qualified experience, retraining, and regression evaluation can extend what the next candidate can justify.
* **Admission can preserve success:** A minimally corrected proposal can complete useful work; proposer autonomy, task success, and protection require separate measures.
* **Restrictions need evidence:** A lower speed still needs traction, clearance, and a feasible response. A stipulated supported branch teaches the release decision without turning illustrative records into measurements.
* **Residual limits select the next experiment:** Missing observations, evaluation support, proof premises, and task scope call for different engineering responses.
:::

A physical AI engineer can carry an intended task through this entire chain. The engineer derives an action envelope from the body and its environment, develops a learned proposer from traceable data, and evaluates that proposer in the closed loop it will inhabit. The engineer then integrates sensing, state, intent, and planning with an independent permission path, measures its timing and fallback behavior, and tests the complete machine under declared operating conditions. The release decision joins useful capability to the evidence that supports it. When evidence is missing, the engineer can identify whether the next step is a measurement, a learning experiment, an architectural change, or a narrower task. That ability to build and justify a machine that senses and acts is the discipline this book develops.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From physical AI to the systems discipline"}
The next unfamiliar machine will bring a different body, task, and environment. Its engineering begins by tracing how observations become proposals and how admitted commands become force, motion, and heat. The methods developed here provide a way to teach useful behavior, integrate it with timely physical control, and determine which operating claims the resulting evidence supports. This work is dedicated to the students, researchers, and systems engineers who take up the challenge of giving machines safe and capable hands in an open physical world.
:::
